newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bundestag passes bill to scrap capital trading tax.
newsitem.headline: Bundestag passes bill to scrap capital trading tax.

text.p: Germany's lower house of parliament on Friday passed a government bill which would scrap a capital trading tax next year, but the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) said they would block the measure in the upper house.
The government's 1996 tax bill was passed by a majority of 330 to 293 in the Bundestag lower house of parliament, voting results showed.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel said that the abolition of the capital trading tax from January 1, 1998 was long overdue.

"We could have abolished the capital trading tax long ago if you in the SPD had not prevented it, and then thousands of people could have been working today," he told the Bundestag. "It belongs in the tax museum."

But the SPD, which voted against the measure, said that the government was playing fast and loose by planning to compensate local governments for lost revenue with a share of a turnover tax without making necessary changes to the constitution.
"You want the Bundestag to pass a law which is clearly unconstitutional," SPD finance spokesman Joachim Poss said. "Even if is constitutional, it violates legislative hygiene."

The capital trading tax is levied only in western Germany, and would have to be introduced automatically in the former communist east if it is not abolished. That Waigel said, would have damaged the capital base of struggling companies there.

He said local governments in the east would be compensated for a loss of 500 million marks in revenue this year through an extra billion marks in low-interest credits made available by development agency the Kreditanstalt fuer Wiederaufbau.
